panel.critic_notes:
1. "Congratulations on financing fifty rounds at a rate our legal team calls generous" is the weakest kind of billing joke, because it never actually says anything cruel about the contestant. Compare the worked example, where the jab lands on the contestant's aim; here the jab lands on the legal team, who are having a fine time. Insincere praise is present, cruelty is not, so it fails Tone rule 1 outright. It also spells out "fifty rounds" in words while the EFFECT line writes "50-round", which reads as sloppy rather than deliberate. And the EFFECT line drops the bleed entirely, which is the only mechanically interesting thing this weapon does.

2. The surcharge is applied to enthusiasm, which is at least a jab at the contestant for being eager, but it is a soft one, and "such enthusiasm deserves" is closer to arch than to insincere praise. Weaker problem in the PLUG, worse problem in the EFFECT: "inflicts 5 damage per second for 3 seconds" omits the word bleed, so a reader cannot tell whether that is the gun's damage output or a separate effect. Given the true behaviour lists rapid fire AND bleed as distinct things, this EFFECT line is ambiguous to the point of being wrong. "Per-trigger-pull" is also three hyphens deep in a line meant to sound like polished broadcast.

3. This one is not on the assigned angle. "You have earned a payout, and we have spent all of it on this crate for you" is a jab about the payout that never arrives, which is in the billing family, but the cruelty is aimed at the Network's own thievery rather than at the contestant, and nothing in the sentence insults them. It is a joke about corporate policy, not about this person. The EFFECT line also drops both the reload and the bleed, keeping only the two least specific facts, and "50 rounds" without "magazine" loses the distinction between a magazine and a total.

4. The strongest of the eight on tone: the Network bills a 1.2 second reload as a rest break, which is fake generosity and contempt in one breath, and "do enjoy" holds the manners. Two real problems. First, "one point two seconds" spelled out is coy in a way the Network's register is not, and it sits directly above the same number as digits. Second, the number in the PLUG makes this the only card where the sales pitch states a mechanical fact, which softens the Type 2 rule 9 gap the whole format depends on.

5. The invoice routes through the crowd and back, which is a decent structure, but "we admire your form so much" is the same insincere-praise opening as the worked example, and the jab never actually names a flaw. Being forwarded a bill is a plot event, not an insult. The EFFECT line is the worst of the eight: it reports "bleed for 5 damage per second" with no duration at all, so the reader is left to assume it is permanent. That is a wrong number by omission, and Type 1 rule 2 counts it as a violation rather than a trim.

6. "A modest Underdog weapon for a modest balance, which is now considerably less modest" is the only proposal that does both halves cleanly, and it lands the jab on the contestant's finances specifically. It is also 87 characters, which is inside the limit but leaves nothing for a proofreading pass, and the triple "modest" is one repetition past witty into pleased-with-itself. The bigger issue is that it leans on the crate tier as a joke about the contestant's status, which reads as a status jab dressed as a money jab. The EFFECT line is the cleanest of the set.

7. "You are such a thorough shopper" is the single best insincere-praise clause in the batch, because thoroughness is the thing that costs the contestant money. But the first half breaks the format's core gap: "bleed damage is charged by the second" puts the mechanic in the sales pitch and the sales pitch in the mechanic, so the flat EFFECT line underneath has nothing left to reveal. It also invites the reader to check whether they are charged for 3 seconds or indefinitely, which is a question the card cannot answer.

8. Restructuring debt "around the Cyber-Swarmers we expect you to reach" is close to the worked example's move, and the implication that the contestant will not reach many of them is genuinely cruel while staying mannered. The problem is "expect you to reach" is doing too much lifting through implication, and a reader could plausibly take it as the Network being confident in them, which flips the joke. The EFFECT line drops the bleed, which matters here because bleed is what makes this weapon good against low-health Cyber-Swarmers, so the card names the counter without giving the reason.

scores.note: The jab lands on the legal team rather than the contestant, so there is insincere praise without cruelty, and spelling out "fifty rounds" above "50-round" reads sloppy.

panel.critic_notes:
1. "Barely used, and only lightly cried on" is the joke, and it aims at a contestant who is only implied as dead, but the bigger problem is that the sarcasm and the cruelty are not in the same breath: this is a single wry aside about a previous owner, with no jab landing on the contestant now holding it. Nothing here says anything about *you*. Strip the game words and it is a used-car gag that would sit in any comedy shooter. The EFFECT line is also the weakest of the eight, dropping "horizontal" and "red-mist" and all of the knockback, which is the part of the behaviour that actually changes how the contestant plays.

2. "Reached wave four" is a naming violation. The approved term is Escalation Tier, and "wave" is not on the list as shorthand for it, so the card is measuring progress in units this show does not use. "You have a lovely target" is also badly built: the intended read is presumably that wave four is a low bar and the contestant should aim to beat it, but as written the sentence says the previous contestant is the target, which is a confused image. The EFFECT drops the reload entirely, which is the one number that matters on a 5-shell tube.

3. This one has the strongest polish and the weakest content. "The grip perfectly moulded, and we do mean perfectly" is coy about a corpse and lands closer to menace than to broadcast, because the joke asks the audience to picture a death grip rather than an invoice or a ranking. It also never mentions the contestant at all, so there is no jab, only an insinuation. Worse, it says "our previous owner", which reads as the Network owning the shotgun, exactly backwards from the second-hand-off-a-casualty angle. And "we do mean perfectly" is a nudge-nudge construction, not corporate polish.

4. "Much like several of tonight's hostiles" is the sharpest lore hook of the eight, since it correctly ties the recycled weapon to the recycled contestants. But the jab still misses the contestant standing there. Nothing in the sentence costs *them* anything, and the sarcasm is thin, because "recovered, polished and returned to service" is not insincere praise, it is accurate. The EFFECT line is also underspecified: it gives only the Cyber-Boar interaction and none of the spread, tube or reload, so a contestant reading it does not learn what the weapon fires.

5. "You are the ninth contestant this season to be handed this exact crate" is the only proposal whose jab lands squarely on the contestant, and the mock congratulation plus the implication that the previous eight are gone is doing both halves. Two real faults. The PLUG is 92 characters, over the 90 limit, so it fails format outright. And "the ninth this season" is a lore fact the card is inventing about the Network's season structure, which no source establishes.

6. The clean joke of the set structurally, and the one that most reads as a threat rather than a broadcast. "We have every confidence it will outlive you" is the Network stating the contestant's death directly, with no manners over the top and no financial or ranking cushion, which is the failure the guide describes as menace over comedy. It is also cruel-and-sincere rather than sarcastic: the Network means every word of it. That is precisely the case Type 2 rule 1 rejects.

7. "Handle with pride" is a good corporate opener and "right up to the end" is the right kind of understatement. The problem is "a bankrupt former contestant", which mis-fires the lore: in this game a bankrupt former contestant who took chassis mods is a *hostile*, so the card implies the shotgun's last owner is currently on the arena floor shooting back, which the line does not intend and does not follow through on. The jab also never touches the contestant, and "kept it spotless" praises the dead one instead of insincerely praising the living one.

8. "You hold it far better than the last contestant did" is exactly the insincere praise the brief wants, and "though she did reach Tier six" is the jab, undercutting the compliment with a record the contestant has not matched. Two defects. "Tier six" is loose for Escalation Tier 6, and given that the guide treats a wrong number as a rules violation rather than taste, an invented tier number for an unnamed predecessor is a fact the card is making up. The EFFECT also says "five pellets per shell" where the true behaviour is five pellets per shot from a five-shell tube, and it drops the 2.5 second reload.

scores.note: "Barely used" is fake generosity and "lightly cried on" is the cruelty, in one breath and aimed squarely at the predecessor the assigned angle permits; the critic's demand that the jab hit the current contestant overreaches the brief, and the leaner EFFECT still agrees with true behaviour, though omitting knockback loses the most playable fact.

panel.critic_notes:
**1.** "Congratulations, your winnings" presupposes winnings, which the Network's whole gag is that it never issues, so the joke undercuts its own premise: it reads as though the contestant has money, which softens the cruelty rather than sharpening it. "Thirty-six payments" is a car-finance reference that lands generically, and it is a joke about the future rather than a jab at the contestant. The EFFECT drops "stationary," which the true behaviour makes load-bearing, since the beam only threads Ranged Sentinels that are standing still.

**2.** "A marksman of your calibre" is the strongest insincere-praise opening in the set, but the sentence then wanders into a joke about the optics rather than about the contestant, so the jab lands on the equipment and nobody gets hurt. "Premium optics deserve a deposit" is a corporate quip that would sit in any store menu in any game. The EFFECT also throws away the piercing beam, the one genuinely distinctive property of this weapon, and lists only reload cosmetics.

**3.** "Charging you rent for every second of that reload" is the best financial construction here, but "we admire your patience" is not really praise, it is a slightly grumpy observation, so the insincerity is thin. Worse, the EFFECT line breaks its own remit: "a sharp sonic crack" is flavour, and this line is supposed to go dead flat, so the joke gap the format depends on narrows.

**4.** This one is nearly all machinery. "Rising Star pricing, generously applied" is corporate texture with no praise of the contestant in it, and "a payout we have never issued" is a fact about the Network, not a jab at the person holding the rifle. It is a good line for a terms-and-conditions screen and a weak one for a card that is meant to insult somebody. The EFFECT drops the word "lines," losing that the beam threads several Sentinels rather than one.

**5.** "Your account balance did not qualify you for the second one" is a real jab, correctly aimed at money, but there is no insincere praise anywhere in the sentence, so it is cruel-and-sincere, which the style guide names as an outright failure mode. It is also the closest thing here to plain contempt rather than broadcast manners. The EFFECT is the weakest of the eight: it lists the laser sight and the reload and never mentions that the beam pierces anything.

**6.** "Such a tidy shot" is faint, condescending praise rather than the grand insincerity the Network trades in, and "itemised on your invoice" is the same billing beat as several others without a distinguishing turn. The bigger problem is the tense: it praises a shot the contestant has not fired yet, on a card that flashes at pickup, so the line is describing something that has not happened.

**7.** "Your debt has been restructured around this very fine rifle" is the sharpest financial idea in the set, because it makes the gift itself the mechanism of the trap. The weakness is the front half: "Delightful news, contestant" is manners without praise, so the insincerity is carried by tone alone rather than by a compliment that curdles. The EFFECT crams four clauses in and reads as a spec sheet, which is arguably correct for this format but sits right at the edge of listing everything rather than saying anything.

**8.** The jab targets an audio effect, not the contestant, so nothing lands on the person at all, and "the Network bills per crack" is a joke about pricing absurdity of the kind that would fit any satirical shop. "Splendid crack you hear" also praises the gun rather than the contestant. On top of that it uses "the Network" in a line spoken by the Network, which reads as a third party describing them rather than the broadcast voice itself.

scores.note: "Congratulations" plus a thirty-six-payment finance plan is a clean sarcasm-plus-money pairing, but the critic is right that "your winnings" grants the contestant a payout the Network never issues, and the EFFECT drops "stationary," which the true behaviour makes load-bearing.

Scrupulous corporate theatre does not admit the trick in the same breath as the signature. It also reads closer to open taunting than to broadcast politeness, and at 98 characters the PLUG breaks the 90-character limit outright, which is a hard format violation before tone is even weighed.

2. "Clause nine, which voids ammunition on wave completion" invents a mechanic that contradicts the true behaviour: the launcher runs dry because six rockets is all it holds, not because a clause deletes ammunition when the wave ends. That is a wrong-behaviour violation in the PLUG, and it also poisons the EFFECT line by implying a rule the EFFECT does not state. "A rare talent like yours deserves" is serviceable insincere praise, but the jab lands on a fictional clause rather than on the contestant, so the cruelty is diffuse.

3. "Our lawyers adore you" is the strongest opening of the eight, and the paperwork angle is properly aimed. The weakness is "resupply request": nothing in the fiction says the contestant ever filed one, so the line invents an offscreen event to make its joke work. "Non-refundable section" is also slightly limp, since nothing was refundable and no money is mentioned, which drains the specificity that would tie it to this show rather than any corporate parody.

4. "Please initial here" is exactly the right register and the line is comfortably inside the limit. The problem is that the jab is generic contempt: "the six rockets you are about to waste" could be said about any weapon in any game, and it is closer to plain insult than to sarcasm, since the Network is not saying the opposite of what it means anywhere in the sentence. Strip the paperwork opener and nothing insincere remains, which means Type 2 rule 1 is only half satisfied.

5. "Arbitration, which we hold after your run" is the sharpest paperwork conceit here, and the death jab is implied rather than stated, which keeps it a joke. "Any dispute about the seventh rocket" also assumes the contestant already knows there are only six, which the card is in the act of telling them.

6. This is the flattest of the eight. "The smallest quantity permitted" is technically the paperwork angle but there is no jab at the contestant at all: the cruelty is aimed at the Network's own stinginess, which makes it corporate self-deprecation rather than hostility. "Your paperwork was flawless" is praise with nothing insincere underneath, since the paperwork presumably was flawless. Sarcastic but harmless, which the guide names as an explicit failure.

That crosses from played-for-laughs into stated threat, and it takes the assigned angle off target at the same time. "Complimentary" and "itemised on your balance" is the right collision, but "gift-shop rate" is the weak link: a gift shop is not a game-show broadcast fixture, and the phrase drifts toward generic theme-park comedy rather than the Network's contract language. The card also never touches the fact that this item is what saves the contestant's life, so the pitch is billing them for lunch, not for a rescue. It clears the rules and lands as a mild joke, which is the problem: mild.

2. "Sixty easy payments you will never live to make" is a death jab wearing a finance costume, and the brief assigns this card the money angle "and nowhere else." The instalment framing is only the delivery vehicle; the punchline is that the contestant dies. It also breaks the register in rule 4: "you will never live to make" is the Network saying the quiet part out loud, which reads closer to a threat than to broadcast copy. The worked example never states the outcome, it lets the audience infer it, and this line refuses to do that.

3. The construction is correct and the "persistence surcharge" is properly absurd corporate invention, but the sentence is a pun that repeats its own keyword: "admire your persistence" then "persistence surcharge" is the joke explaining itself inside 90 characters. Sharper cards let the second half surprise the first. Also, "persistence" is generic praise that could attach to any item in the game, so this PLUG is not really about a turkey leg or a Death Save at all. Swap it onto the Sponsor Aegis and nothing changes, which means it is not doing item-specific work.

4. This one has a real defect. "A generous 25% off your remaining health" states the mechanic backwards: the item restores 25%, it does not discount health, and framing it as a percentage off makes it sound like a reduction. Reading it as a sales-discount joke still puts a number in the PLUG that fights the number in the EFFECT, and constraint 1.2 makes number agreement a violation rather than a preference. The second half, deducting from a payout no contestant has claimed, is the strongest financial jab in the set, so the line is worth rebuilding around that clause and dropping the discount conceit entirely.

5. Cruel and financially targeted, but the sarcasm is thin: tripling a premium is straightforwardly hostile, with only "Congratulations, contestant" carrying the insincerity, and that opener is doing all the work alone. Rule 2.1 wants both in the same breath, not a sincere jab with a polite hat on. There is also a lore problem: "Death Save insurance" invents a Network product, and constraint 1.1 bans invented names, no generic substitutes, in a card whose whole purpose is proving these terms are canon. Naming Death Save is good; selling insurance on it is not sanctioned.

6. The itemised-delivery gag is well-observed and "disposal" is the best word on this list, because it is the death jab implied through a line item rather than stated, which is exactly the inference the worked example relies on. The weakness is structural: "The Network covers the poultry" is a statement of generosity, not insincere praise of the contestant, so there is no jab aimed at them personally, only at their wallet. It is also the least polished sentence rhythmically, three nouns in a list, which reads as a receipt rather than as broadcast patter. Closest to sound of the eight, but the flattery is missing.

7. "What a bargain" is fake enthusiasm rather than fake praise of the contestant, and "one quarter of you, restored" is a genuinely good echo of the mechanic. But "one half of everything you own" is a number, and constraint 1.2 is about the EFFECT line agreeing with real behaviour, so an invented 50% asset seizure sits in the PLUG unbacked by anything in the game. More damaging: the contestant entered with crushing debt and owns nothing, so half of everything they own is nothing, and the joke's premise collapses on the lore it is built on.

"Purely so the catering looks free to viewers" is the Network protecting its broadcast image at the contestant's expense, which is the specific flavour of corporate hostility the guide asks for, and rounding up a balance is precisely mundane in the way real invoicing is. The one soft spot is that there is no insincere praise of the contestant at all: it is cruelty plus corporate polish, and rule 2.1 wants mock congratulation or fake generosity in the mix. The fix is small, since "purely so the catering looks free" already implies fake generosity; making that gift explicit in the first clause would close it.

"Invoiced to your estate" is a death jab, and this card was assigned money, so it smuggles in the wrong angle under financial vocabulary. 1. "You signed for these, and clause nine says the cold was your idea all along." The jab is present but the praise is missing entirely, so the sarcasm collapses into flat blame. Nothing here is insincere praise, fake generosity or mock concern; it is just the Network telling the contestant it is their own fault, which is cruel-but-sincere, the exact failure mode the guide calls out. "The cold was your idea" also drifts toward mocking the item rather than the contestant, and "you signed for these" is the weakest possible paperwork gesture, available to any game with a shop.

2. "Congratulations on qualifying, subject to terms no contestant has lived to dispute." The congratulation carries the mock-praise, but the jab is a death jab dressed in a legal clause, and the assigned angle is paperwork. "Terms no contestant has lived to dispute" only works because of the dying, not because of the terms; strip the word "terms" and the joke is unchanged, which proves the paperwork is decoration. It also spends the card's variation budget on the joke every other card can already tell.

3. "Non-refundable, as the crowd agreed on your behalf during the last commercial break." Two angles fighting: non-refundable is paperwork, the crowd enjoying itself is the crowd variation, and neither lands cleanly because the sentence splits its weight. This is the Network taunting, not selling; "Do enjoy" is fake generosity, thin but real, yet the payload is a straightforward you-will-not-survive-long sneer with no financial or contractual bite. The small print is a prop, not the jab. It also reads closest to menace of the eight, because "the closest you will get to a rest" points directly at the contestant's death with nothing corporate softening it.

5. "Your waiver was so thorough that the Network has nothing left to feel sorry about." Strongest of the set and the objection is narrow: "so thorough" praises the paperwork, not the contestant, so the mock-praise lands one step off target. Polished and on-angle, but there is no praise, sincere or otherwise, so it is administrative cruelty rather than sarcasm. "Cleared no time on your calendar" is also a death implication wearing a scheduling costume, so it quietly borrows the variation angle again. The construction "we have cleared no time" is stiff enough that the joke has to be decoded rather than heard, and a card flashes on screen for an instant.

panel.critic_notes:
1. "Congratulations on inheriting the sidearm of a contestant who also had faith in it" is the safest possible reading of the brief and reads like a first draft. The jab is entirely carried by the word "also," which is a one-syllable hinge doing all the work; a reader skimming a card that flashes on screen for a second will miss it completely. "Inheriting" already telegraphs the death, so "also had faith in it" adds nothing except a second, weaker gesture at the same idea. The EFFECT line is a bare four-item spec list with no verb, which is fine as flatness but omits the fallback behaviour, the one fact that actually distinguishes this weapon from every other blaster in every other shooter.

2. This is the one proposal that stops being a broadcast and starts being a threat. "Not by anyone you will meet" is a menacing implication delivered with a straight face, and Constraint 2.6 rules out menace explicitly. Worse, "the grip is already worn to a comfortable shape" is faintly grim in a tactile, bodily way, drifting toward the horror register rather than the game-show one. There is also no insincere praise anywhere in the sentence, so it fails 2.1 on the sarcasm half: it is cruel and sincere, which the rule names as an outright failure. Strip the game name off this card and it could sit in any post-apocalyptic looter.

3. The number is invented. "Escalation Tier four" is a specific factual claim about a previous contestant's run that nothing in the brief supports, and the card is not licensed to fabricate history with numbers in it when Constraint 1.2 treats wrong numbers as violations. Spelling it "four" instead of 4 also breaks the register of a corporate readout. "You have a target to admire" is the wrong flavour of cruelty as well: it is condescending rather than sarcastic, and it accidentally lands as something like encouragement, which 2.5 forbids. The joke is also inert, since reaching Tier 4 is not obviously pitiful to a first-time contestant who has no idea what a good tier is.

4. "The eighth is now a Cyber-Boar" is the sharpest line here and also the most likely to be wrong on lore. The hostiles that were formerly contestants are the ones who took chassis mods as a severance package; asserting that a dead contestant became a specific quadruped hostile is a claim the brief does not license, and Cyber-Boar in particular reads as an animal chassis rather than a severance upgrade. "You are the ninth contestant to hold this" is also flat statement, not praise, so the sarcasm half of 2.1 rests on nothing. It is a good joke attached to a factual assertion the show may not be able to make.

5. Closest to functional, and still soft. "Loved this weapon dearly" is genuine insincere praise of the item rather than the contestant, which is a half-step off the rule: 2.1 wants the jab landed on the contestant, and this one lands on the deceased instead, leaving the current contestant as a bystander to someone else's joke. "Right up until the very end" is the most generic euphemism available and would work unaltered in any game with a body count. "Very" is padding in a 90-character line that should be spending every character.

6. "We polished off the last contestant" is a botched pun. The intended reading is polishing the weapon, but "polished off the last contestant" idiomatically means the Network killed them, which turns a broadcast pleasantry into an on-air murder confession, and that collapses the gap between manners and content that 2.4 says the comedy depends on. Once the Network says the cruel part out loud there is nothing left for the audience to work out. The EFFECT line also drops "unlimited ammo" where the canon phrasing is infinite ammo, and "standard fallback sidearm" quietly repeats the ITEM name back at the reader.

7. Two problems, one fatal. "His" assigns a gender to a hostile the brief never genders, and the Ranged Sentinel is the long-range robot, not one of the chassis-modded former contestants, so "used to be a contestant" is a straight lore error. The line is also 89 characters against a 90 limit with no praise in it at all, so it spends its whole budget on a factual claim that is wrong. "This was his favourite too" is the same "previous owner liked it" beat as proposals 1 and 5, told less well.

8. The strongest of the eight, and it still has a seam. "It has come back to us every single season, which is more than we can say for its owners" is properly sarcastic in structure, keeps the corporate manners intact, and lets the audience do the arithmetic, which is exactly what the worked example does. The flaw is aim: the jab targets "its owners," a group the contestant is only implicitly joining, so the cruelty arrives at the contestant second-hand rather than direct. It is also 94 characters, over the 90-character ceiling, which is a hard format violation and not a rounding error.
